methods.name: block.close
methods.description: Close a block and end the program running in it.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

block_id.description: The block to close. It may be a detached block. Send this or window_id, not both.

window_id.description: The window whose focused block to close. It doesn't have to be the active window. Send this or block_id, not both.

keep_last.description: If true, fail rather than close the only block left in a window, counting floating layers. Ignored for detached blocks.

block_id.description: The block that closed.

revision.description: The session's revision after this call. It is unchanged if the block was detached, because a detached block isn't part of the view.

validation_notes: Send exactly one of `block_id` and `window_id`. If you send both, or neither, the call fails with `bad_request`.
The server sends `block_closed` when the block closes. If it was the last block in its window, the window closes too and the server sends `window_closed`.
If `keep_last` is true and the block is the only one left in its window, counting blocks in floating layers, the call fails with `bad_request` and closes nothing.
If the block's creator is still placing it, the call returns at once and the block closes when placement finishes.

On one connection, `block.close` waits for earlier requests that can change focus, such as `session.new_split` and `session.focus_block`, to finish. A close by `window_id` therefore closes the block those requests left focused.

If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` or `window_id` names something that isn't in the session, or the window has no focused block, it fails with `not_found`.

methods.name: block.event
methods.description: Send an input event, such as a key press or a paste, to a block.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

block_id.description: The block to send the event to.

type.description: The kind of event, such as key, paste, mouse, wheel, or focus.

payload.description: The event's fields. Leaving it out is the same as an empty object.

event.description: The event to send: its type, such as paste, and its payload.

validation_notes: A client may send only `key`, `paste`, `mouse`, `wheel`, and `focus` events. Every other event type is sent only by the server. A `paste` event's `payload` is `{"text": "..."}`, and a `focus` event's `payload` is `{"action": "in"}` or `{"action": "out"}`.
The event goes straight to the block, so Lua key bindings never see it. To give key bindings the first chance at a key, use `client.key` instead.
On one connection, `block.event` calls run one at a time, in order with `client.key`, so the block receives events in the order you send them.
The call returns once the block has received the event, which may be before the block has finished acting on it.

The call fails with `bad_request` if `event` is missing or its `payload` has the wrong shape for its type. It also fails with `bad_request` if `event.type` is empty, names an event only the server sends, or names an event this server doesn't know.
If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`, and if `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`.

methods.name: block.method
methods.description: Call a method that a block provides and return its result.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

block_id.description: The block to call the method on.

method.description: The block method's short name, such as write or format.

args.description: The block method's own arguments. Leaving it out is the same as an empty object.

validation_notes: Send the block method's short name, such as `write`, in `method`. `help.all` lists the methods each creator's blocks provide under `block_types`, with each method's `args_schema` and `output_schema`.

Each block method can also be called by its full name, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, with the same `session_id`, `block_id`, and `args`. The full name names the block's creator, so the call works only on a block that creator made. On any other block, it fails with `conflict`.
The result is the block method's own result, as its `output_schema` describes it. `block.method` has no result schema of its own.

`block.method` doesn't wait for earlier requests on the same connection, and it can run at the same time as `client.key`. If a call depends on an earlier request, wait for that request's reply first. To call a block method in order with `client.key`, such as from a key binding, use `client.action`.

If `block_id` is missing, the call fails with `bad_request`. If the session doesn't exist, it fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`, and if the block has no method named `method`, it fails with `method_not_found`. If `args` is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type, it fails with `bad_request`.

methods.name: block_creator.list
methods.description: List the creators the server can make blocks with, and their flavors.

name.description: The creator's name, such as com.superlogical.terminal.

title.description: A short name for people to read, such as Terminal.

description.description: A sentence about what the creator's blocks do.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account its blocks run as. If it equals your local server's host_id, its blocks see the same files you do.

name.description: The flavor's short name within its creator, such as shell.

flavor.description: The flavor's full name, such as com.superlogical.terminal.shell. Use it in the flavor field of session.new_block or a layout.

title.description: A short name for people to read, such as Shell.

description.description: A sentence about what this flavor creates.

options_schema.description: A JSON Schema for the options this flavor accepts.

events.description: The block events, by name. Each value is a JSON Schema for the event's fields.

methods.description: The block methods, by short name.

input_schema.description: A JSON Schema for the method's arguments.

output_schema.description: A JSON Schema for the method's result.

name.description: The action's short name, such as reset. Its full name, used in key bindings, is the creator's name, a dot, and this name.

title.description: The name to show a person, such as Reset Terminal.

description.description: A sentence about what the action does, to show under its title in a menu or command palette.

category.description: A group of related actions, such as Pane.

keywords.description: More words to search for the action by, separated by spaces.

args.description: The fixed arguments the method is called with when the action runs. Left out when there are none.

repeats.description: True if holding the key down should run the action again, as holding an arrow key does.

actions.description: The actions that call this method, in the order the creator declares them.

api.description: The methods and events that this creator's blocks provide.

features.description: Optional features the creator supports. Ignore names you don't know. No names are defined yet.

creators.description: Every creator available, with its flavors and the API its blocks provide.

validation_notes: Creators are sorted by `name`.
To create a block, pass a flavor's `flavor` to `session.new_block` or in the `block` of a layout, with `options` that match its `options_schema`.

`api.methods` lists the methods that every block from the creator provides. Call one as `<creator>.<method>`, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.title`, with `session_id`, `block_id`, and its arguments under `args`.

A method's `actions` are things a person can do with a block, such as choosing an item in Rex.app's command palette or pressing a key. Performing one calls the method with the action's `args`, which are fixed values, not a schema like the `args` that `client.keymap` lists for an action.

methods.name: client.action
methods.description: Perform an action from the configuration file or a block, as this client.

action.description: The full name of the action, such as dev_layout or com.superlogical.terminal.reset. client.keymap lists them.

args.description: The action's arguments, as a JSON object. Leave it out if there are none, and always for an action a creator declares.

origin.description: What caused the request: key, palette, or api (the default). The action reads it as ctx.origin. Other values count as api, but script makes the call fail with bad_request.

session_id.description: The session the action applies to. Required for a block action. A configuration file action may leave it out, and then has no default session.

block_id.description: The block the action applies to. Defaults to the session's focused block, unless server is set. Requires session_id.

name.description: The name an action uses for the server, in rex.server(name) and ctx.server. It must be unique and not empty.

id.description: Any non-empty value the client uses to recognize the server. It comes back unchanged in client_call_requested events.

servers.description: Other servers this client is connected to, which a configuration file action can call with rex.server(name). Don't list the server you're sending this to.

server.description: The name, from servers, of the server that holds session_id and block_id. Leave it out when they're on the server you're sending this to.

result.description: The block method's result, or what the configuration file action returned. Left out if that action returned nothing, nil, or true.

action.description: The name of the client action to perform. Ignore a name you don't know.

args.description: The action's arguments, as a JSON object. Left out if there are none.

client_actions.description: Actions the configuration file action asked this client to perform with rex.client.queue, in order. Perform each one as you would a key binding.

ordered_after.description: The id of the request this connection ran just before this one, counting only methods that run in order, such as client.key. Left out if there was none.

validation_notes: `action` decides what runs. A name without a dot, such as `dev_layout`, is an action that the configuration file defines with `rex.action`. A name with a dot, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset`, is an action or method of a block, named after its creator. `client.keymap` lists every name in `actions`.

A block action, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset`, has fixed arguments, so a request for one with `args` fails with `bad_request`. A block method, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, takes its arguments from `args`.
If `args` isn't an object, the call fails with `bad_request`. `null` counts as leaving it out.
The client's own actions, such as `pane.split`, run in the client and can't be sent here. A request for one, or for any name the server doesn't know, fails with `not_found`.

On each connection, `client.key`, `client.action`, `block.event`, and the methods that change focus or the layout run one at a time, in the order they arrive. For an action bound to a key, use this method rather than calling the block method by name, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, so the action takes effect after the keys typed before it.

When `session_id` is set, the connection must be attached to that session, with `session.attach`, `session.bootstrap`, or `session.attach_all`, or the call fails with `conflict`. If `session_id` names no session, the call fails with `session_not_found`. Neither check applies when `server` is set.

Send `session_id` with any block action or method, and whenever you send `block_id`, or the call fails with `bad_request`. A block action or method runs on `block_id`, or on the session's focused block if you leave that out. If the session has no focused block, the call fails with `conflict`.
If the block isn't the kind the action or method belongs to, the call fails with `conflict`. If `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`.

An action from the configuration file may leave out `session_id`. It then has no `ctx.session_id`, and its `rex.session` calls have no default session. With `session_id`, it sees `block_id`, or the focused block, as `ctx.block_id`.
If `origin` is `script`, the call fails with `bad_request`, because only `rex.invoke` may report that origin.

An action from the configuration file may run for 30 seconds, including time spent waiting on other servers. If it runs longer, the call fails with `timeout`. If the file is reloaded while it runs, the call fails with `conflict`.

If an action from the configuration file raises an error, the call fails with a message that starts with where it happened, such as `init.lua:4: attempt to index a nil value`. However the action fails, part of it may already have run.

Each entry in `servers` needs a unique, non-empty `name` and a non-empty `id`, and `server` must name one of them. Otherwise the call fails with `bad_request`. The server doesn't interpret either value.

Set `server` when the session belongs to one of `servers`. The IDs then go to the action unchecked, and the focused block isn't filled in, so send `block_id` yourself. The action's `rex.session`, `rex.block.call`, and `rex.call` calls go to that server.
When `server` is set, any name with a dot fails with `bad_request`, because a block action must run on the server that holds the block. Send it to that server instead.

When the action calls another server, this connection receives a `client_call_requested` event. Make the call there and report the outcome with `client.reply`. If no reply comes within 10 seconds, or the reply is an error, the action's call fails and the action keeps running.

methods.name: client.inspect
methods.description: Get one connected client's details, including the actions it offers.

client_id.description: The client to describe. It can be any client, not only the one calling.
The client's ID. It stays the same when the client reconnects.

kind.description: What sort of program the client is: app, cli, agent, or other. Left out if the client didn't say. Treat a kind you don't know as other.

platform.description: What the client runs on: macos, ios, linux, windows, freebsd, web, or other. Left out if the client didn't say. Treat a platform you don't know as other.

name.description: The program's name, such as Rex.app or rex.

version.description: The program's version, as the program prints it, such as 1.6.0.

label.description: The client's label, such as studio. Two clients can share a label.

info.description: What the client says about itself, such as its name and version, for showing to people. Left out if it said nothing.

kind.description: How the server identified the client: 'peer' (Unix socket credentials), 'windows_peer' (named pipe credentials), 'tailscale' (a Tailscale login), or 'anonymous' (not identified). Show a kind you don't know by its name.

transport.description: How the client first reached Rex: 'unix', 'named_pipe', 'tcp', or 'tailscale'. A login server passes it on unchanged.

display.description: A readable name for the client, such as uid 501 or alice@example.com. It can be out of date or shared, so compare uid, sid, or user_id instead.

remote_addr.description: The client's network address. Left out when there is none, such as on a Unix socket.

uid.description: The client's Unix user ID. Only for kind peer.

gid.description: The client's Unix group ID. Only for kind peer.

pid.description: The client's process ID when it connected, for kind peer or windows_peer, if known. Process IDs are reused, so use it only for debugging.

sid.description: The client's Windows security identifier, which survives account renames. Only for kind windows_peer.

user_id.description: The Tailscale user ID that owns the client's device. Only for kind tailscale. Check tags before treating it as a person.

login_name.description: The client's Tailscale login name, usually an email address. For display only.

node.description: The name of the client's Tailscale device. Only for kind tailscale.

tags.description: The Tailscale tags of the client's device. Any tag means the client is a machine, such as a CI runner, not a person.

path.description: The route the client took to this server, for troubleshooting. Entries include 'tailscale' (built-in Tailscale), 'tailnet' and 'tailnet-serve' (the machine's own Tailscale), and 'login-server' (passed on by a login server).

principal.description: Who the client is, as the server identified it when it accepted the connection.

connected_at.description: When the client first connected, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. It doesn't change when the client reconnects.

connection_state.description: Whether the client has a connection: connected, or lost if it dropped and the client may still reconnect. Treat a missing or unknown value as connected.

connection_lost_at.description: When the server noticed the connection drop, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. Set only while connection_state is lost.

session_ids.description: The sessions the client attached to with session.attach or session.bootstrap, sorted by ID. Left out if there are none.

client.description: The client, as client.list describes it.

name.description: The name that bindings use for the action, such as pane.split. Names from the configuration file never contain a dot.

kind.description: What performs the action: client (the client itself), lua (a rex.action in the configuration file), or block (a block of the creator that the name starts with).

title.description: The name to show a person, such as Split Pane.

description.description: A sentence about what the action does, to show under its title in a menu or command palette.

category.description: A group of related actions, such as Layouts. Configuration file actions without one are filed under Actions.

keywords.description: More words to search for the action by, separated by spaces.

args.description: A JSON Schema of the arguments the action takes. Left out when the action doesn't describe any.

repeats.description: True if holding the key down should run the action again, as holding an arrow key does.

source.description: Where the action is defined, as file:line, such as init.lua:12. Left out when there's no location, as for every action a client declares.

actions.description: The actions the client declared in its latest client.keymap request that listed any. Left out if it declared none.

validation_notes: If `client_id` is missing or isn't a client ID, the call fails with `bad_request`. If it names no connected client, including one that has left, the call fails with `not_found`.
To ask the client to perform one of the actions in `actions`, call `client.perform`.

methods.name: client.key
methods.description: Send a key to a block, giving Lua key bindings the first chance at it.

session_id.description: The session the key is typed in.

key.description: The physical key, named after its W3C KeyboardEvent code in snake_case, such as key_a for KeyA, the A key on a US keyboard. It doesn't change with the keyboard layout. Any other key is unidentified.

mods.description: The modifier keys held down, joined with + in this order: shift, ctrl, alt, super, caps_lock, num_lock, shift_side, ctrl_side, alt_side, super_side. On a Mac, super is the Command key. The lock names mean the lock is on, and a name ending in _side means the right-hand key of that pair is held. An empty string means none.

consumed_mods.description: The modifiers the keyboard layout used to produce text, such as shift for a capital letter. Written like mods, which also includes them.

text.description: The text the key typed. Empty for keys that type nothing, such as arrows and modifiers.

unshifted_codepoint.description: The Unicode code point the key types without shift, such as 110 for n. Bindings such as ctrl+n match on it, so they follow the keyboard layout. 0 if none.

composing.description: True while the key is part of an unfinished composition, such as a dead key or an input method.

action.description: What happened to the key: press, release, or repeat while it's held down.

key.description: The key event, as the keyboard reported it.

block_id.description: The block to send the key to. Defaults to the session's focused block.

prefix.description: The keys pressed before key when key ends a key sequence, in order. For ctrl+b then x, send x as key and ctrl+b here.

handled.description: True if a Lua function in the client's script or the configuration file took the key. No block received it then.

validation_notes: The connection must be attached to `session_id`, with `session.attach`, `session.bootstrap`, or `session.attach_all`, or the call fails with `conflict`. If `session_id` names no session, the call fails with `session_not_found`.

Without `block_id`, the key goes to the session's focused block. The server reads it once, before any Lua function runs, so a function that moves focus doesn't change where the key goes. Either way, Lua functions see the block the key goes to as `ctx.block_id`.

On each connection, `client.key`, `client.action`, `block.event`, and the methods that change focus or the layout run one at a time, in the order they arrive. That keeps keys in the order you send them.
The key goes first to the Lua functions bound to it in this client's scripts, then to those in the configuration file. If none of them takes the key, it goes to the block.

Only a key bound to a Lua function reaches Lua, and only when it's pressed or repeating. Every other key goes straight to the block. `client.keymap` reports the bound keys as bindings for `client.key.forward`.
If no Lua function takes the key and the session has no focused block, the key goes nowhere. The call still succeeds, with `handled` set to false.
To send a key sequence, wait until it's complete. Then send its last key as `key` and the keys before it in `prefix`, such as `["ctrl+b"]`. The server doesn't remember keys between requests.
A key with a `prefix` reaches only the functions bound to that exact sequence. A key without one reaches only the functions bound to that key alone.
If no function takes a key sequence, only `key` goes on to the block. The keys in `prefix` never do.
A Lua function bound to a key may run for 5 seconds. If it raises an error or runs longer, the call fails and the key doesn't reach the block.
If an element of `prefix` isn't a key the server can read, the call fails with `bad_request`, and the message names the element.
If no Lua function takes the key and `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, the call fails with `not_found`.

methods.name: client.keymap
methods.description: Get what each key does for this client. The result combines the client's own bindings with the configuration file and the client's Lua scripts.

name.description: The name that bindings use for the action, such as pane.split. Names from the configuration file never contain a dot.

kind.description: What performs the action: client (the client itself), lua (a rex.action in the configuration file), or block (a block of the creator that the name starts with).

title.description: The name to show a person, such as Split Pane.

description.description: A sentence about what the action does, to show under its title in a menu or command palette.

category.description: A group of related actions, such as Layouts. Configuration file actions without one are filed under Actions.

keywords.description: More words to search for the action by, separated by spaces.

args.description: A JSON Schema of the arguments the action takes. Left out when the action doesn't describe any.

repeats.description: True if holding the key down should run the action again, as holding an arrow key does.

source.description: Where the action is defined, as file:line, such as init.lua:12. Left out when there's no location, as for every action a client declares.

actions.description: The actions the client performs itself. Leave it out to skip the checks for unknown actions and wrong arguments. The server keeps the list for client.inspect and client.perform.

server_actions.description: Which of the server's actions the reply lists: all (the default), configured (only the configuration file's), or none. An unknown value means all.

name.description: The layer's name, such as default or settings, which its bindings report as their source. Unique in the request, with no colon.

keys.description: The keys that trigger the binding, such as cmd+k, or cmd+[KeyK] for a key by its position. A key sequence has one element per key, in the order pressed.

action.description: The name of the action to run.

args.description: The arguments to run the action with, as a JSON object, exactly as the user wrote them. Left out if there are none.

source.description: Where the binding came from: a layer name, such as default, or a file:line, such as init.lua:12. Ignored in a request.

mode.description: The mode the binding belongs to, such as resize. The binding applies only while that mode is active. Left out for a binding outside every mode.

bindings.description: What the layer binds, in the order it bound them. A later binding sits above an earlier one on the same key.

keys.description: The keys to clear, spelled like a binding's keys. Only the same spelling matches. Empty, with mode set, to remove that whole mode.

action.description: The one action to take off the keys, such as pane.split. Leave it out to clear the keys whatever is bound to them.

mode.description: The mode to remove the keys from. Leave it out for keys outside every mode. With empty keys, it removes the whole mode.

removals.description: What the layer takes off the layers beneath it. Removals never touch the layer's own bindings.

defaults.description: The client's built-in layers, lowest first. They sit beneath the configuration file. Problems found only in them aren't reported, because the user can't edit them.

name.description: The layer's name, such as default or settings, which its bindings report as their source. Unique in the request, with no colon.

keys.description: The keys that trigger the binding, such as cmd+k, or cmd+[KeyK] for a key by its position. A key sequence has one element per key, in the order pressed.

action.description: The name of the action to run.

args.description: The arguments to run the action with, as a JSON object, exactly as the user wrote them. Left out if there are none.

source.description: Where the binding came from: a layer name, such as default, or a file:line, such as init.lua:12. Ignored in a request.

mode.description: The mode the binding belongs to, such as resize. The binding applies only while that mode is active. Left out for a binding outside every mode.

bindings.description: What the layer binds, in the order it bound them. A later binding sits above an earlier one on the same key.

keys.description: The keys to clear, spelled like a binding's keys. Only the same spelling matches. Empty, with mode set, to remove that whole mode.

action.description: The one action to take off the keys, such as pane.split. Leave it out to clear the keys whatever is bound to them.

mode.description: The mode to remove the keys from. Leave it out for keys outside every mode. With empty keys, it removes the whole mode.

removals.description: What the layer takes off the layers beneath it. Removals never touch the layer's own bindings.

overrides.description: Layers of shortcuts a person recorded in the client, lowest first. They sit above the configuration file and this client's scripts. Problems in them come back as warnings.

keys.description: The keys that trigger the binding, such as cmd+k, or cmd+[KeyK] for a key by its position. A key sequence has one element per key, in the order pressed.

action.description: The name of the action to run.

args.description: The arguments to run the action with, as a JSON object, exactly as the user wrote them. Left out if there are none.

source.description: Where the binding came from: a layer name, such as default, or a file:line, such as init.lua:12. Ignored in a request.

mode.description: The mode the binding belongs to, such as resize. The binding applies only while that mode is active. Left out for a binding outside every mode.

bindings.description: The resolved bindings, in the order to try them. When several share a key, run the first one whose action is available.

severity.description: How serious the problem is: warning, for something the user probably didn't mean, or error, for a part that was skipped. Show a value you don't know as a warning.

source.description: Where the problem is, as file:line, such as init.lua:22. Left out when it isn't known.

message.description: The problem in one sentence, ready to show. Its wording may change, so don't parse it.

action.description: The full name of the action the problem is about, as written, even if misspelled. Left out if it isn't about one action.

key.description: The key the problem is about, spelled like a binding's keys, with a sequence joined by spaces, such as ctrl+a b. Left out if it isn't about one key.

mode.description: The mode the problem is about. Left out if it isn't about a mode.

diagnostics.description: Problems to show the user, such as a binding to an action that doesn't exist. Empty when there are none.

name.description: The name that bindings use for the action, such as pane.split. Names from the configuration file never contain a dot.

kind.description: What performs the action: client (the client itself), lua (a rex.action in the configuration file), or block (a block of the creator that the name starts with).

title.description: The name to show a person, such as Split Pane.

description.description: A sentence about what the action does, to show under its title in a menu or command palette.

category.description: A group of related actions, such as Layouts. Configuration file actions without one are filed under Actions.

keywords.description: More words to search for the action by, separated by spaces.

args.description: A JSON Schema of the arguments the action takes. Left out when the action doesn't describe any.

repeats.description: True if holding the key down should run the action again, as holding an arrow key does.

source.description: Where the action is defined, as file:line, such as init.lua:12. Left out when there's no location, as for every action a client declares.

actions.description: The server's actions that keys can be bound to: the configuration file's, then each creator's, by creator name. Left out when there are none.

name.description: The mode's name, such as resize. Its bindings have it as their mode, and client.mode.enter takes it as its name argument.

exclusive.description: True if keys the mode doesn't bind are ignored while it's active. If false, they do what they do outside the mode.

blocked.description: Keys that must not reach the bindings outside the mode while it's active. If the mode also binds one, that binding still runs. Each is spelled like a binding's keys.

modes.description: Every mode in the keymap, sorted by name. Left out when there are none. The client decides which mode is active.

path.description: The absolute path of the configuration file, whether or not it exists.

exists.description: True if the file existed when the server last read it.

generation.description: How many times the server has loaded its configuration file since it started, counting from 1. It goes up even when the file didn't change, so compare hash and instance_id, not this, to tell whether a keymap you kept is current.

instance_id.description: The ID of the server process, as server.status reports it. A new value means the server restarted, so send your client.set_script scripts again.

hash.description: The SHA-256 of the configuration file and the modules it requires while it loads, in lowercase hexadecimal. Empty if there's no file or it couldn't be read.

config.description: The configuration file the keymap came from. Present even when the file doesn't exist, so you can tell the user where to create it.

validation_notes: Bindings stack in layers, from bottom to top: your `defaults`, then the account's configuration file, then the scripts this client loaded with `client.set_script`, then your `overrides`.
A layer's `name` becomes the `source` of its bindings and of warnings about it. If a name is empty, contains a colon, or is used by another layer in either list, the call fails with `bad_request`.

The keymap is always the calling client's, so a request that includes `client_id` fails with `bad_request`. So does a top-level `bindings` list, which older servers accepted. Send those bindings as a layer in `defaults` instead.

A key sequence such as ctrl+b followed by c is `["ctrl+b", "c"]` in `keys`. The configuration file writes it as `ctrl+b>c`, but the result always lists the keys separately. The server doesn't split an element such as `ctrl+b>c`. It treats it as a key it can't read.
Keys the server can read come back in their standard spelling. `cmd+d` and `cmd+[KeyD]` are still different keys: the first follows the keyboard layout and the second names a physical key.

A key spelling the server can't read is kept as written, in either list, so a newer client keeps its keys. Only a removal with the same spelling can take it off. A sequence with any such key is kept the same way.

A sequence sits on the stack of its first key, in order among that key's other bindings. If the top binding a client can perform is a sequence, the client waits for the next key. The server keeps no state between keys, so waiting is the client's job.

A key bound to a Lua function, in the configuration file or this client's scripts, comes back as a binding for `client.key.forward`. To perform it, send the key to `client.key`. Treat it as always available: the bindings below it on that key never run, even when no function takes the key.

For a sequence bound to a function, send its last key to `client.key` with the earlier keys in `prefix`. The binding ends the stack only for that exact sequence, so other sequences that start with the same key still work.

A key can't both run a binding of its own and start a sequence, so the higher of the two wins. The server keeps both and adds one warning per key, with the `source`, `action`, and `key` of the binding that can't run. It warns even about a binding in `defaults`, unless the one above it is in `defaults` too.
A removal matches keys in full. Removing `["ctrl+b"]` leaves every sequence that starts with ctrl+b, and removing `["ctrl+b", "c"]` leaves ctrl+b.
A removal that removes nothing gets a warning, unless it's in `defaults`, names a key the server can't read, or blocks a key in a mode.

A binding or removal with a `mode` belongs to that mode, a set of bindings the client uses only while the mode is active. If a mode name contains anything but lowercase letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, or is `root`, the call fails with `bad_request`.

Bindings in a mode stack and are checked like any others. A key in a mode never hides the same key outside it, and a removal affects only its own mode. The configuration file writes a key in a mode as `resize/left`.
`modes` lists a mode if any layer binds a key in it, blocks a key in it, or declares it with `rex.mode`.
A removal in a mode that names no `action` always blocks its key, so the key is listed in the mode's `blocked`, whether or not anything was removed. A removal that names an action never blocks.

A removal with a `mode` and no `keys` removes the whole mode: its bindings, its blocked keys, and its declarations in the layers beneath. If it also names an `action`, the call fails with `bad_request`.
Above a removed mode, a layer that binds, blocks, or declares a key in the mode brings the mode back, with only what that layer and the ones above it say. Otherwise the mode isn't in `modes`.
The client decides which mode is active, with its own `client.mode.enter`, `client.mode.exit`, and `client.mode.exit_all` actions. The server keeps no mode state.
The server warns about a `client.mode.enter` binding whose `name` argument isn't a mode in the keymap, and about a declared mode with nothing bound in it.
An empty request returns the bindings of the configuration file and this client's scripts, without checking for unknown actions or wrong arguments.

When `actions` isn't empty, the server adds its own actions before checking: those the configuration file defines with `rex.action`, every block method, and every block action. A binding to one of these is never reported as unknown.

A binding with wrong arguments is kept, with a warning. A binding to a block method must pass arguments that match the method's input schema, and passing none counts as `{}`. A binding to a block action, or to a method with no input schema, must pass no arguments.

A binding to an action from the configuration file must match the `args` schema the action declares, if it declares one. The client's own actions aren't checked, because the client checks their arguments itself.

`actions` in the result lists the configuration file's actions in the order it defines them, then each creator's methods and block actions, sorted by creator and then by method name. It doesn't repeat the actions you sent.
A block method in `actions` has no `title`, and its `args` is its input schema. Bind it, but don't show it in a menu. A block action has a `title` and no `args`.
`server_actions` changes only what `actions` lists in the result, not which actions bindings are checked against.
To show a diagnostic next to the binding it's about, match its `action`, `key`, and `mode` to the binding's.

A client can keep using a stored result while its request is unchanged and `config.instance_id` and `config.hash` both match. Call this method again after every `client.set_script` call, and after every `keymap_changed` event whose `hash` differs from the stored one.

methods.name: client.list
methods.description: List the clients connected to the server, in the order they connected.

session_id.description: List only the clients attached to this session with session.attach or session.bootstrap.

kinds.description: List only the clients of these kinds, such as app. A client that didn't report a kind matches none.

client_id.description: The client's ID. It stays the same when the client reconnects.

kind.description: What sort of program the client is: app, cli, agent, or other. Left out if the client didn't say. Treat a kind you don't know as other.

platform.description: What the client runs on: macos, ios, linux, windows, freebsd, web, or other. Left out if the client didn't say. Treat a platform you don't know as other.

name.description: The program's name, such as Rex.app or rex.

version.description: The program's version, as the program prints it, such as 1.6.0.

label.description: The client's label, such as studio. Two clients can share a label.

info.description: What the client says about itself, such as its name and version, for showing to people. Left out if it said nothing.

kind.description: How the server identified the client: 'peer' (Unix socket credentials), 'windows_peer' (named pipe credentials), 'tailscale' (a Tailscale login), or 'anonymous' (not identified). Show a kind you don't know by its name.

transport.description: How the client first reached Rex: 'unix', 'named_pipe', 'tcp', or 'tailscale'. A login server passes it on unchanged.

display.description: A readable name for the client, such as uid 501 or alice@example.com. It can be out of date or shared, so compare uid, sid, or user_id instead.

remote_addr.description: The client's network address. Left out when there is none, such as on a Unix socket.

uid.description: The client's Unix user ID. Only for kind peer.

gid.description: The client's Unix group ID. Only for kind peer.

pid.description: The client's process ID when it connected, for kind peer or windows_peer, if known. Process IDs are reused, so use it only for debugging.

sid.description: The client's Windows security identifier, which survives account renames. Only for kind windows_peer.

user_id.description: The Tailscale user ID that owns the client's device. Only for kind tailscale. Check tags before treating it as a person.

login_name.description: The client's Tailscale login name, usually an email address. For display only.

node.description: The name of the client's Tailscale device. Only for kind tailscale.

tags.description: The Tailscale tags of the client's device. Any tag means the client is a machine, such as a CI runner, not a person.

path.description: The route the client took to this server, for troubleshooting. Entries include 'tailscale' (built-in Tailscale), 'tailnet' and 'tailnet-serve' (the machine's own Tailscale), and 'login-server' (passed on by a login server).

principal.description: Who the client is, as the server identified it when it accepted the connection.

connected_at.description: When the client first connected, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. It doesn't change when the client reconnects.

connection_state.description: Whether the client has a connection: connected, or lost if it dropped and the client may still reconnect. Treat a missing or unknown value as connected.

connection_lost_at.description: When the server noticed the connection drop, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. Set only while connection_state is lost.

session_ids.description: The sessions the client attached to with session.attach or session.bootstrap, sorted by ID. Left out if there are none.

clients.description: The clients, in the order they first connected. An empty list, never null, when none match.

validation_notes: With no arguments, the result lists every connected client, including short-lived ones such as the `rex` CLI.

`session_id` counts only clients attached to that session with `session.attach` or `session.bootstrap`. A connection that only called `session.attach_all` doesn't count. Any client may use this filter, attached or not.
In `kinds`, a kind this server doesn't know counts as `other`. A client that didn't report a kind matches no filter, not even `other`.

If a client's connection drops without closing, the client stays in the list for up to 60 seconds, with `connection_state` set to `lost`, so it can reconnect. A client that wasn't attached to anything and had no scripts leaves at once.
To keep a copy of this list up to date, call `session.attach_all` with `event_scope` set to `all`. The connection then receives `client_joined`, `client_left`, and `client_changed` events.

methods.name: client.perform
methods.description: Ask another client to perform one of its actions and wait for its answer.

client_id.description: The client to ask. To find one by its label, call target.resolve with kinds set to client.

action.description: The name of an action the client declared, such as pane.split. client.inspect lists them.

args.description: The action's arguments, as a JSON object. Leave it out if there are none.

origin.description: What caused the request, such as key, palette, api, or cli. The client receives it unchanged. Empty means api.

session_id.description: The session the action applies to, if any. The client receives it without the server checking it.

block_id.description: The block to act on instead of the client's focused block, if any. The client receives it without the server checking it.

timeout_ms.description: How long to wait for the answer, in milliseconds, once the client is sent the request. Defaults to 10000. Values over 30000 count as 30000.

result.description: What the client's action returned. Left out if it returned null, as most actions do.

performed_by.description: The client that performed the action. It is always the client that client_id named.

validation_notes: The server sends the named client a `client_perform_requested` event and waits for it to answer with `client.reply`.
The server tells the named client which client asked, based on the connection the request arrived on, so a client can't claim to be another.
The connection doesn't need to be attached to `session_id`, because the server only passes it on to the client.
Requests to one client wait in line, and the client answers them one at a time in the order they arrived. `timeout_ms` counts from when a request reaches the front of the line.

A request without `client_id` or `action`, with a negative `timeout_ms`, or with `args` that aren't an object or don't match the action's schema fails with `bad_request`. If `client_id` names no connected client, the call fails with `not_found`.
If the client has listed its actions and `action` isn't one of them, the call fails with `not_supported`. A client that listed none is asked anyway, and it may answer `not_supported` itself.
A client that declines answers `refused`, and the call fails with that code and a message that says why.
If the client is reconnecting, already has 16 requests waiting for it, or disconnects while the request waits, the call fails with `client_unavailable`.
If the client doesn't answer in time, the call fails with `timeout`. The client isn't told, so it may still perform the action later.

When a request ends, the server sends a `client_performed` event with the outcome to connections that called `session.attach_all` with `event_scope` set to `all`. A request that names no connected client sends no event.

methods.name: client.reply
methods.description: Answer a client_call_requested or client_perform_requested event.

call_id.description: The call_id of the event you're answering.

result.description: The call's result, or what the action returned. Use null if there is none. Set this or error, not both.

code.description: The kind of failure, as an error code such as not_found, refused, or internal.

message.description: What went wrong, written for people.

error.description: Why the call failed or the action wasn't performed. Set this or result, not both.

validation_notes: A `client_call_requested` event asks this client to make one call on another server, for a `client.action` request that is still running. Reply to every one, even when the call fails. Send the event's `call_id`, on the connection that received the event.

A `client_perform_requested` event asks this client to perform one of its own actions for another client's `client.perform` request. Reply the same way. `result` is what the action returned, or `null`.
A reply that sets both `result` and `error`, or neither, fails with `bad_request`. For a call with no result, send `"result": null`.
For a call that failed, use the code and message the other server returned, or explain why you couldn't make the call. The waiting action sees only the message.
For an action you didn't perform, set `error.code` to `not_supported`, `refused`, or `internal`. The client that sent `client.perform` gets that code unchanged. An empty code is sent as `internal`.

A reply runs as soon as it arrives. It doesn't wait behind this connection's earlier `client.key` and `client.action` requests, because a `client.action` request that is waiting for the reply holds that line.
A `call_id` that nothing is waiting for fails with `not_found`. That includes a call that was already answered and one that timed out.

methods.name: client.set_label
methods.description: Set or remove this client's label.

label.description: The label to set, such as studio. An empty string removes it. At most 64 bytes, with no control characters.

validation_notes: The label always belongs to the client that sends the request. A request that includes `client_id` fails with `bad_request`.
The server removes whitespace from both ends of `label` before it checks the label, so a label of only spaces removes the current one.
A label longer than 64 bytes, or one that isn't valid UTF-8 or contains a control character, fails with `bad_request`. The message says which rule it breaks.
Labels don't have to be unique. Two clients with the same label are told apart by their IDs.
Labels are for people to read. The server never uses one to decide what a client may do.
When the label changes, the server sends a `client_changed` event to connections that called `session.attach_all` with `event_scope` set to `all`.

A client can also send a label when it connects, in the `client` field of its `hello` message. The same rules apply, but the server fixes the label instead of failing: it cuts a label longer than 64 bytes down to size and drops one that is otherwise invalid.

methods.name: client.set_script
methods.description: Load Lua scripts for this client, replacing any it loaded before.

name.description: A file name to show in error messages and diagnostics, such as init.lua.

scripts.description: Every Lua source to load, run in order. They replace all the scripts loaded before. An empty list unloads them.

items.description: A key binding: modifiers, then a key, joined with +, such as ctrl+n or cmd+left. The modifiers are ctrl, alt, shift, and cmd, always in that order. A bracketed key, as in ctrl+[KeyN], names a key by its position, using its W3C KeyboardEvent code. Other keys follow the keyboard layout.

bindings.description: The single keys the scripts bind to Lua functions. A key sent alone reaches the scripts only if it's listed here and pressed or repeating. Key sequences aren't listed.

all_keys.description: Never sent by this server. If an older server sends true, send every key to client.key, not only those in bindings.

severity.description: How serious the problem is: warning, for something the user probably didn't mean, or error, for a part that was skipped. Show a value you don't know as a warning.

source.description: Where the problem is, as file:line, such as init.lua:22. Left out when it isn't known.

message.description: The problem in one sentence, ready to show. Its wording may change, so don't parse it.

action.description: The full name of the action the problem is about, as written, even if misspelled. Left out if it isn't about one action.

key.description: The key the problem is about, spelled like a binding's keys, with a sequence joined by spaces, such as ctrl+a b. Left out if it isn't about one key.

mode.description: The mode the problem is about. Left out if it isn't about a mode.

diagnostics.description: Problems in the scripts, written to show the user. The server skips each line it can't carry out and loads the rest.

validation_notes: The scripts belong to this client and apply in every session it's attached to. A request that includes `session_id` or `client_id` fails with `bad_request`.
If a script has a syntax error, raises an error, or runs longer than 5 seconds while it loads, the call fails with `bad_request`. The scripts loaded before keep running.
To see every key and key sequence the scripts bound to a function, call `client.keymap`. It reports each one as a binding for `client.key.forward`.

The keys that reach the scripts are fixed when they load. A function that a script binds later, while it runs, receives a key only if a function was already bound to that key or sequence when the scripts loaded.

A successful call can still return `diagnostics`, even with severity `error`. An error marks a part of a script the server skipped, such as a binding to a key it can't read. The rest of the scripts still load.
Loading scripts changes this client's keymap without a `keymap_changed` event. Call `client.keymap` again after each call to this method.

methods.name: data.connect
methods.description: Get a one-time ticket for opening a data connection to a block. A data connection streams a block's content as it changes, such as a terminal's output.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block. The connection must be attached to it with session.attach or session.bootstrap.

block_id.description: The block that provides the data.

data_ref_id.description: Which of the block's data sources to open, such as terminal.

subprotocol.description: The subprotocol the data connection will use, such as rex.data.terminal.v1. If set, the ticket works only on a connection that uses it.

ticket.description: A single-use ticket to send in the HELLO message that opens the data connection. Only a data connection from the same user can use it.

expires_in_ms.description: How long the ticket stays valid after the server issues it, in milliseconds.

validation_notes: The connection must be attached to `session_id` with `session.attach` or `session.bootstrap`. `session.attach_all` isn't enough. If the connection isn't attached, the call fails with `conflict`.
To use the ticket, open a WebSocket to `/api/data` on the server and send the ticket in the HELLO message. A ticket works once, even if the handshake fails, and expires after `expires_in_ms`.
If another user presents the ticket, the data connection gets REJECT reason 0x01, as it would for an unknown ticket. The ticket is then used up, so your own data connection can't use it either.
The server checks only that `data_ref_id` is well formed. If the block has no data by that name, the server closes the data connection with WebSocket status 1008 after the handshake.

Set `subprotocol` to the subprotocol the data connection will use, such as `rex.data.terminal.v1`. The server then refuses a data connection that uses a different one with REJECT reason 0x07, before any data is sent.
If `subprotocol` is left out, the block checks the subprotocol after the handshake and closes the data connection with status 1008 if it doesn't support it.
The call fails with `bad_request` if `data_ref_id` or `subprotocol` is malformed, and with `not_found` if the block isn't in the session or has no data to offer.

methods.name: help.all
methods.description: Describe every method the server provides, including block methods.
validation_notes: The result has two lists. `methods` describes each method with its arguments, result, examples, and notes. `block_types` lists each creator whose blocks provide methods, with its flavors and those methods.
The result describes the server you are connected to, so it always matches that server's version.
Over HTTP, `GET /api/help` returns the same document with an added `http` field, and `/llms.txt` shows it as Markdown.

methods.name: hosts.list
methods.description: List the server's hosts: the other Rex servers you connect to by label.

id.description: The host's ID, such as host:<uuid>, chosen by the device that adds the host. If hosts.put leaves it out, the server creates one.

label.description: The name you connect to the host by, such as studio. Unique in the list, ignoring case, and at most 64 characters.

endpoints.description: The addresses that reach the host, in the order to try them, such as studio.tail1234.ts.net. Each takes a form the -S option of rex accepts.

icon.description: The name of an icon for clients to show next to the label. Rex doesn't interpret it.

host_id.description: The host_id that the host's server.status reported when the host was added, if known. Compare it with a server's host_id to tell whether this host is that server.

added_from.description: The device or client that added the host. For display only.

updated_at.description: When the host last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. The server sets it and ignores any value a client sends.

source.description: Where the configuration file declares the host, such as init.lua:12. Left out for a host added with hosts.put. The server sets it.

hosts.description: Every host in the list, sorted by label, ignoring case, then by id. An empty list when there are no hosts.

hash.description: Identifies this version of the list. hosts.put, hosts.remove, and the hosts_changed event report the same hash for the same list.

severity.description: How serious the problem is: warning, for something the user probably didn't mean, or error, for a part that was skipped. Show a value you don't know as a warning.

source.description: Where the problem is, as file:line, such as init.lua:22. Left out when it isn't known.

message.description: The problem in one sentence, ready to show. Its wording may change, so don't parse it.

action.description: The full name of the action the problem is about, as written, even if misspelled. Left out if it isn't about one action.

key.description: The key the problem is about, spelled like a binding's keys, with a sequence joined by spaces, such as ctrl+a b. Left out if it isn't about one key.

mode.description: The mode the problem is about. Left out if it isn't about a mode.

diagnostics.description: Warnings about the hosts declared in the configuration file. Left out when there are none. The hash doesn't cover them.

validation_notes: Every Rex server keeps a host list. Each of your devices reads its hosts from the one server it uses as its home, so they all see the same list.

The list holds the hosts declared with `rex.host` in the server's configuration file, and the hosts that clients added with `hosts.put`. A declared host has a `source`, such as `init.lua:4`. A host added with `hosts.put` has none.
Each host comes back exactly as it was stored, including fields this server doesn't know. A client that sends a host back with `hosts.put` must keep those fields.
A declared host with a mistake in it, or whose label another host already uses, is left out of `hosts`. A warning in `diagnostics` names the line that declared it.
A server started without a state directory can't store hosts, so it lists only the declared ones.
If a hand edit broke the file that stores the hosts, the call fails with `conflict` and a message that names the file.

methods.name: hosts.put
methods.description: Add a host to the server's host list, or replace the host with the same ID.

id.description: The host's ID, such as host:<uuid>, chosen by the device that adds the host. If hosts.put leaves it out, the server creates one.

label.description: The name you connect to the host by, such as studio. Unique in the list, ignoring case, and at most 64 characters.

endpoints.description: The addresses that reach the host, in the order to try them, such as studio.tail1234.ts.net. Each takes a form the -S option of rex accepts.

icon.description: The name of an icon for clients to show next to the label. Rex doesn't interpret it.

host_id.description: The host_id that the host's server.status reported when the host was added, if known. Compare it with a server's host_id to tell whether this host is that server.

added_from.description: The device or client that added the host. For display only.

updated_at.description: When the host last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. The server sets it and ignores any value a client sends.

source.description: Where the configuration file declares the host, such as init.lua:12. Left out for a host added with hosts.put. The server sets it.

host.description: The host to add, or to store in place of the host with the same id.

id.description: The host's ID, such as host:<uuid>, chosen by the device that adds the host. If hosts.put leaves it out, the server creates one.

label.description: The name you connect to the host by, such as studio. Unique in the list, ignoring case, and at most 64 characters.

endpoints.description: The addresses that reach the host, in the order to try them, such as studio.tail1234.ts.net. Each takes a form the -S option of rex accepts.

icon.description: The name of an icon for clients to show next to the label. Rex doesn't interpret it.

host_id.description: The host_id that the host's server.status reported when the host was added, if known. Compare it with a server's host_id to tell whether this host is that server.

added_from.description: The device or client that added the host. For display only.

updated_at.description: When the host last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. The server sets it and ignores any value a client sends.

source.description: Where the configuration file declares the host, such as init.lua:12. Left out for a host added with hosts.put. The server sets it.

host.description: The host as the server stored it, with its id and updated_at.

hash.description: Identifies the list after the call, the same way hosts.list does.

validation_notes: The device that adds a host chooses its `id`, so sending the same request again is safe and adds nothing. If `host` has no `id`, the server creates one.
If `host` matches the stored host in every field except `updated_at`, nothing changes and the result holds the stored host.

`label` can't be empty, can't start or end with white space, and has at most 64 characters. No other host in the list may have the same label, ignoring case. If one does, the call fails with `conflict` and a message that names that host and, for a declared host, the line that declared it.
`endpoints` needs at least one endpoint, each in a form that the `-S` option of `rex` accepts. Unix sockets and named pipes aren't allowed, because their paths work only on their own machine.

To change a declared host, put a host with its `id`. The server never writes the configuration file. It stores the host you send, which takes the place of the declared one. A put also brings back a host that `hosts.remove` removed.
The server sets `updated_at` and drops `source`. It stores every other field as sent, including fields it doesn't know.
When the put changes the list, every connected client receives a `hosts_changed` event.

If `host` fails a check, the call fails with `bad_request` and a message that names the field. A server started without a state directory can't store hosts, and fails with `not_supported`. A hand edit that broke the file that stores the hosts makes the call fail with `conflict`.
The file that stores the hosts can hold at most 1 MiB, which is room for thousands of hosts. A put that would make it larger fails with `too_large`.

methods.name: hosts.remove
methods.description: Remove a host from the server's host list.

removed.description: True if the host was in the list before the call and isn't now. False if there was nothing to remove.

hash.description: Identifies the list after the call, the same way hosts.list does.

validation_notes: Removing a host that isn't in the list isn't an error. `removed` is false, nothing changes, and no event is sent, so calling it again is safe. The same happens if `id` is left out.

The server never writes the configuration file, so removing a declared host hides it. Removing a stored host that took the place of a declared one removes both. Either way, only a later `hosts.put` with the same `id` brings the host back.
When a host is removed, every connected client receives a `hosts_changed` event.

If `id` isn't a valid host ID, the call fails with `bad_request`. A server started without a state directory can't store hosts, and fails with `not_supported`. A hand edit that broke the file that stores the hosts makes the call fail with `conflict`.

methods.name: server.apple.grant_file_access
methods.description: Let the server, and every program it runs, read files a Mac app was given.

path.description: The file's absolute path. If it names a directory, access covers everything inside it.

token.description: A macOS sandbox extension token for path, which the app gets from sandbox_extension_issue_file. The server uses it only if it can't already open path.

files.description: The files to make readable, in the order they were dropped or pasted. At most 256.

access.description: 'readable' if the server could already open the file, 'granted' if it can now because it used the token, or 'denied' if it still can't. Treat a value you don't know as 'denied'.

message.description: Why access was denied, written for a log. The wording can change, so check access instead.

files.description: One result for each requested file, in the same order as the request.

validation_notes: A Mac app calls this when a file is dropped on or pasted into a terminal. macOS lets the app open the file, but not always the server, which macOS treats as a different app.
For each file, the server first tries to open `path`. It uses `token` only if it can't, so most files, such as those in a project, come back `readable` and their tokens go unused.
A file the server can't open doesn't fail the call. A relative path is always `denied`.
Access lasts until the server exits. If a file comes back `denied`, or with an `access` value the client doesn't know, copy the file somewhere the server can read instead.
A request that names more than 256 files fails with `bad_request`.

Only the server can read its own permissions. A Mac app calls this to show them, and calls it again after the person changes one in System Settings.
Reading the permissions never makes macOS ask the person anything.

methods.name: server.config_reload
methods.description: Reload the configuration file and tell every client to fetch its keymap again.

generation.description: How many times the server has loaded its configuration file since it started, counting this load. It goes up on every load, even one that fails.

severity.description: How serious the problem is: warning, for something the user probably didn't mean, or error, for a part that was skipped. Show a value you don't know as a warning.

source.description: Where the problem is, as file:line, such as init.lua:22. Left out when it isn't known.

message.description: The problem in one sentence, ready to show. Its wording may change, so don't parse it.

action.description: The full name of the action the problem is about, as written, even if misspelled. Left out if it isn't about one action.

validation_notes: The server reads the same configuration file it read when it started, usually `init.lua`, along with the modules that file loads with `require`.
The next `client.keymap` result reports the same `generation` in `config.generation`, unless the file is reloaded again first.

A mistake that stops the file from loading, such as a Lua syntax error, doesn't fail the call. The server keeps the bindings, actions, and hosts from the last load that worked, and `diagnostics` reports the mistake.
If the file no longer exists, the reload removes the bindings, actions, and hosts it used to declare. That isn't an error.

methods.name: server.stop
methods.description: Shut the server down, or with if_idle, only if nothing is using it.

if_idle.description: Stop only if the server has no sessions and no other client is connected. A server that is in use refuses with conflict and keeps running.

validation_notes: Only a client on the server's own machine, connected over its Unix socket or named pipe, can call this method.
Without `if_idle`, the server stops no matter what it is doing, and every program running in its sessions ends.

With `if_idle`, the server stops only if it has no sessions, including any still being created or closed, and no client is connected except the caller. Otherwise it keeps running and the call fails with `conflict`. The error message says what is using the server.
The server checks and stops in one step. A client that connects just after the check is refused.
The server replies before it shuts down. Close the connection after reading the reply. The server waits up to a second for the connection to close before it stops.
A server running inside another program, with no process of its own, fails the call with `not_supported`.
The server accepts this method only over its local Unix socket, or its named pipe on Windows. Over any other connection, such as TCP or Tailscale, the call fails with status 403.

validation_notes: Built-in Tailscale is a copy of Tailscale inside Rex. It makes the server join your tailnet as a device of its own, so the machine doesn't need Tailscale installed.
If built-in Tailscale is already on, the call only applies `allow_tailnet_members`, without restarting the device or dropping connections. It ignores `hostname`, `auth_key`, and `advertise_tags`.

The first time the device starts, it must sign in to Tailscale. With a valid `auth_key`, it signs in without a browser. Otherwise `state` becomes `needs_login`, and the sign-in link appears in `auth_url` and in the server's log.

The call returns once the device has started, before it has finished connecting. The server is reachable over the tailnet only once `https.state` is `available`. Follow the progress with `tailscale_status_changed` events, on a connection that called `session.attach_all` or `session.bootstrap`.

methods.name: server.whoami
methods.description: Get how the server identified you, and the account the server runs as.

kind.description: How the server identified the client: 'peer' (Unix socket credentials), 'windows_peer' (named pipe credentials), 'tailscale' (a Tailscale login), or 'anonymous' (not identified). Show a kind you don't know by its name.

transport.description: How the client first reached Rex: 'unix', 'named_pipe', 'tcp', or 'tailscale'. A login server passes it on unchanged.

display.description: A readable name for the client, such as uid 501 or alice@example.com. It can be out of date or shared, so compare uid, sid, or user_id instead.

remote_addr.description: The client's network address. Left out when there is none, such as on a Unix socket.

uid.description: The client's Unix user ID. Only for kind peer.

gid.description: The client's Unix group ID. Only for kind peer.

pid.description: The client's process ID when it connected, for kind peer or windows_peer, if known. Process IDs are reused, so use it only for debugging.

sid.description: The client's Windows security identifier, which survives account renames. Only for kind windows_peer.

user_id.description: The Tailscale user ID that owns the client's device. Only for kind tailscale. Check tags before treating it as a person.

login_name.description: The client's Tailscale login name, usually an email address. For display only.

node.description: The name of the client's Tailscale device. Only for kind tailscale.

tags.description: The Tailscale tags of the client's device. Any tag means the client is a machine, such as a CI runner, not a person.

account.description: The operating system account the server runs as. It can differ from your own name. Left out when unknown.

validation_notes: Which fields `principal` has depends on its `kind`. A `peer` has `uid` and `gid`, and usually `pid`. A `windows_peer` has `sid`, and usually `pid`. A `tailscale` client has `user_id`, `login_name`, and `node`, plus `tags` if its device is tagged. An `anonymous` client has none of these.
The server identifies a client when its connection opens. `principal` stays the same for as long as the connection lasts.
`principal` describes a decision the server already made when it let the client in. Use it to show who is connected, not to decide what a client may do.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account the block runs as. If it equals your local server's host_id, the block sees the same files you do. Otherwise treat the block as remote.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

blocks.description: The blocks in the layer, in layout order. The layout field says where each one sits.

layers.description: The window's layers, from back to front. The first is the tiled layer, which holds the window's layout and fills the window.

windows.description: The session's windows, in order. Rex.app shows them as tabs in this order.

view.description: The session's view, read after the connection started receiving its events. Apply it first, then the events whose seq is higher than the response's.

validation_notes: The connection starts receiving every event from the session, including `block_event`, before the server reads `view`. Apply `view` first, then each event whose `seq` is higher than the response's `seq`, even one that arrived before the response.

Most methods that take a `session_id` work only on a connection attached to that session, with this method, `session.bootstrap`, or `session.attach_all`. On a connection that isn't attached, they fail with `conflict`.
Attaching makes the connection's client one of the session's clients. The server sends `client_connected`, and `session.list_clients` lists the client.
`data.connect`, `session.own_block`, and `session.disown_block` need this kind of attachment. Attaching with `session.attach_all` isn't enough for them.
Calling it again for the same session is safe. It returns the same `client_id` and a fresh `view`.
If `session_id` names no session, the call fails with `session_not_found`.

methods.name: session.attach_all
methods.description: Start receiving events from the whole server and get the list of sessions.

event_scope.description: Which events to receive. 'session' sends every session's events except block_event, plus session_created, session_destroyed, session_moved, and tailscale_status_changed. 'all' also sends block_event and the client events, such as client_joined.

sessions.description: Every session on the server when this connection started receiving events.

validation_notes: Use `session` unless you need `block_event` or the client events. With `all`, the client events are `client_joined`, `client_left`, `client_changed`, `client_performed`, and `client_script_events_dropped`. Any value other than `session` or `all` fails with `bad_request`.
The connection still receives every event from a session it attached to with `session.attach`, whatever the scope.

The connection doesn't join any session. It can call methods on every session, but it isn't listed in `session.list_clients` and can't call `data.connect` or own blocks. To join a session too, call `session.attach`, or use `session.bootstrap` to do both in one call.
Calling it again replaces the scope with the new `event_scope`.
The session list is a snapshot taken after events start. Apply each event whose `seq` is higher than the response message's `seq` on top of it.

Events arrive in order, and their `seq` has no gaps. If the connection falls more than 8 MiB of events behind, the server closes it rather than skip events. Open a new connection to get a fresh snapshot.
